text: yeah so the whole point of the final plunge was a controlled crash instead of just running out of gas. the probe had been out there for years, and there was always that risk of it carrying trace Earth microbes or at least the chance of it. if its orbit degraded and it accidentally bumped into a moon like Enceladus or Titan, it could introduce those Earth bugs to a world that actually has liquid water. so they deliberately steered it straight into Saturn's atmosphere to burn it up, keeping the potentially habitable moons clean from any forward contamination. i think that was the main goal.

pretty sure the pain is just your standing leg taking the full bodyweight while the other leg is free to kick. when you push off, the push leg does the work and then relaxes, but the stationary leg stays loaded and bent, so the hip flexors and quad are holding tension for a long stretch. if you ride with that leg locked or too straight, the knee has to absorb every little bump, and if you keep it too bent, the hip and hamstring are doing extra work. after a while those muscles start screaming, which people often mistake for a bad joint or something worse.

another thing that gets overlooked is the way your hips shift side to side on a board. your stance isn't symmetrical when you're actually kicking, so one hip is doing most of the stabilizing while the other is basically just hanging out. that uneven load makes the stationary side get sore faster than the kicking side, even though it looks like it is doing less. it's usually just fatigue and alignment, and it goes away with time.

if it still hurts, check that your board setup isn't making your body twist. too narrow trucks or a board that's too short can force your hips and shoulders into a weird angle, and that kind of strain shows up as hip or knee pain. try widening the stance a little and keep that stationary leg relaxed, not locked. if the pain is sharp, comes on suddenly, or is in the joint instead of the muscles, that's when you'd actually go see someone. for normal after-ride soreness though, it's mostly just muscles being tired from holding the load.

yeah so “Afro-American” isn’t really saying most of them live in Africa, it’s pointing to the African connection, the ancestry and cultural inheritance. a lot of Black Americans trace their roots to West and Central Africa through the transatlantic slave trade, so the label is about where the family history starts, not where the person was born. that’s the bit i think gets missed. and yeah, there is also a political and identity dimension to it, especially from the civil rights era onward, where Black Americans were reclaiming an African identity that had been largely erased over centuries of slavery. so “Afro” functions more like “of African descent” rather than a literal nationality marker. it’s kinda like how “Hispanic” or “Latino” refer to heritage and culture, not current residence. also worth noting, a lot of Black Americans don’t actually use the term much in everyday life; it’s more of a formal or academic label.

yeah so i think the core idea is that the brain treats intense pleasure as a signal, and if you hit that signal too hard too often it starts reshaping. that's why euphoric drugs, even the good ones, come with a catch. the reward system isn't designed for repeated strong hits. after a while you need more for the same feeling, and stopping becomes uncomfortable. so the drug itself isn't the whole story, it's what it does to your baseline. this isn't just about getting high. the nervous system is built to maintain balance, and pleasure is one of the strongest levers it uses to make you keep doing things that matter for survival. push that lever hard and it fights back, so the very circuit that makes the high feel amazing also makes you need more, and makes stopping feel bad.

there's also the body side. anything you put in has to be processed, and that processing costs something. alcohol wrecks the liver, stimulants hit the heart and sleep, opioids change gut function, and some sedatives can make breathing shallow. none of that is random. if a drug makes you feel great, the same pathways that produce that feeling are also the ones that get worn, desensitized, or pushed into dependence. iirc that's why the more powerful the high, the more likely you'll see withdrawal or mood drops when it wears off. people call that the cost, and it's not always pretty.

what you're describing, a strong high with zero downside, would basically be a free reward. but the brain doesn't run on free rewards. it balances itself. too much stimulation and it dials down sensitivity, too little and it pushes the other way. so the same chemistry that gives euphoria also sets up withdrawal. and since people metabolize things differently, what's mild in one person can be a lot in another. dose, age, sex, and even what else is in the body all change the effect. that's why doctors are careful with dosing, and why one size never fits everyone.

i don't think all drugs are bad, i just don't think you get to skip the trade off. you can pick ones that are gentler, use less, and maybe combine with exercise or good habits, but the reward system still adapts. there are drugs with fewer nasty side effects, but zero downside while giving real pleasure is still a long way off.

so house buying is a bit of a minefield but i’ve picked up a few things that might help. First off, always get the property surveyed before you lock in an offer. A lot of people skip this to save time and money, but small issues can turn into huge problems later, and a surveyor can spot stuff like damp, poor plumbing, or roof problems that aren’t obvious.

Also try not to panic about the mortgage. Talk to a broker early, because they can compare deals for you and keep the process moving forward. Don’t just go with your bank’s first offer.

One thing i always forget to mention is checking local council plans. If a new road or housing development is coming, that can affect your property’s value and what it’s like to live there.

And whatever you do, get everything in writing. Verbal agreements don’t really count when it’s time to close the deal.

Let me know if you want help figuring out any of that stuff.

Cheers

so a 3-in-1 is really just one formula trying to do the hair and body jobs at once, while the separate products each do one job properly. the big difference is you lose some dedicated strength in every role. the shampoo part isn't as deep-cleaning, and the conditioner part isn't as strong, because the same ingredients have to be gentle enough for your body too. iirc the cleansers get milder so they don't dry out skin, and that means less hair cleaning and less conditioning. that's also why it's cheaper per use sometimes, not better. the 2-in-1 is only hair focused, so it can use stronger shampoo and stronger conditioner, but it won't double as a bodywash.

tbh the bottle says it saves time, but it won't make your hair feel as soft as a real conditioner, at least that's how it was explained to me. i'd only use it for a couple of days or when you're in a rush. so don't expect the separate products' level of cleaning and conditioning, it's mostly convenience.

yeah so the short version is they basically track the same points on the ground over time using GPS. There are these little receiver units that sit on stable rocks and record the position repeatedly. The GPS satellites give the position in 3D, and by comparing the same spot at different times you get the speed and direction the ground is moving. It's kinda like a time-lapse of the whole planet.

The tricky bit is that moving the ground moves the point too, but they correct for that using the satellite network. There's also a system called VLBI which uses radio telescopes and quasars as background markers. I'm pretty sure that's the stuff geophysicists actually use for the fine measurements.

So you end up with numbers like centimetres per year, and it adds up a lot over millions of years. It's not super precise on a single day, but the longer the baseline the clearer the trend gets.

Inbreeding doesn't lower IQ directly in a simple way, but it increases the chance that two recessive harmful gene variants show up together in the same child. Everyone carries a few such hidden variants. When two related people have kids, the shared ancestry means those variants are more likely to match up on both copies of a gene.

For intelligence, some of those harmful variants affect genes involved in brain development and function. So the offspring aren't just "getting a lower IQ" because of the relationship itself; it's the higher chance of double-dosing a deleterious mutation.

That's the core idea. It's not every child, not every couple, and not just one gene. The effect shows up more strongly as the family tree narrows, which is why close relatives mating tends to produce more of these hidden problems.

Carbon monoxide is dangerous because of what it does inside the blood. When you breathe, oxygen binds to a protein called hemoglobin in red blood cells, and those cells carry the oxygen out to every tissue in the body. Carbon monoxide also binds to hemoglobin, but it grabs on about 200 times more strongly than oxygen does. Because the binding is so much stronger, carbon monoxide crowds the oxygen out, and the blood ends up carrying far less oxygen than it should. Tissues then start to starve, and even though you keep breathing in normal air, the oxygen can't get where it needs to go.

That's the main reason it's so poisonous. A smaller amount of carbon monoxide can cause headaches, dizziness, and weakness; in high enough concentrations it can knock you out or even prove fatal, especially in a closed space where the gas accumulates.

Carbon dioxide behaves differently. Your body produces it as a waste product, and your lungs constantly flush it out. Under normal conditions you aren't poisoned by it. It only becomes a problem when the concentration gets very high, because then it simply pushes the air out of your lungs, so there's less oxygen available. That's a different mechanism from carbon monoxide, which actively takes over the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood.

So in short: carbon dioxide is mostly a quantity issue, while carbon monoxide is a binding issue. It steals the oxygen transport system and quietly makes the body short on oxygen, which is why even modest exposure can hurt you without much warning.

so the whole point of bracing is basically stopping your body from shooting forward on impact. when the plane hits something or stops suddenly, you keep going because of momentum, and that's what hurts you. the brace position is about tucking the head down against something solid, so it doesn't whip around and hit the seat or the wall. you bend the knees, point the feet, and get the head down. it helps with the deceleration part, so your body slows down more evenly instead of slamming into a surface.

it's not just about one thing though. you also need to tuck your feet flat and keep them in contact with the floor so your lower body doesn't flip forward too. the idea is to shorten the distance your body travels before impact. and honestly, the easiest way to do it right is to practice a bit. you don't want to be figuring it out in the middle of a crash.

I've been buying and financing cars for years, and I keep seeing this exact confusion, so let me sort it out. The dealer's advertised low rate is almost always part of a package where you're paying for extras you didn't ask for, and that's where the savings vanish.

When a dealer promotes a low APR, that rate is tied to the whole deal. The car itself is priced higher than the same model you'd finance through a bank, and the dealer bundles in things like extended warranties, GAP coverage, and service contracts. You might get 4.99% instead of 6.5%, sure, but the starting price on the car might be a few hundred dollars higher, and the add-ons can tack on another thousand or two. Once you add it all up, the lower rate stops mattering because you're borrowing more money and paying for fees you never asked for.

A bank gives you a clean loan. You tell them what you need, and they quote a fixed APR and total cost without trying to sell you a bundle. You control the loan amount, so you're not paying interest on money you didn't ask for, and there's no markup hidden in the car price.

Here's the part nobody tells you: the low rate is a hook. The dealer's profit isn't really in the loan, it's in the car price and the extras. The interest savings are real but small, while the price gap and the bundled products are much bigger, so they swallow any interest you thought you saved. The bank wins on total cost even when its sticker rate looks worse, because you're not forced to buy the add-ons and the inflated price.

The practical move is to compare total cost, not just the APR. Get a loan quote from your bank or credit union, then ask the dealer for an out-the-door price with every add-on listed. If the dealer's total is higher, the lower rate didn't save you anything, because you paid more for the car and the extras.

That's my take after too many car purchases: trust the bank, and make the dealer show their full price.

its wild thinking about how a chemical imbalance keeps you alive. so the way our body makes electricity is mostly about chemical gradients pushing ions around. think of it like a chemical pump. cells move sodium out and pull potassium in, setting up a charge difference across the membrane. imo the heart is the best example of this. its pacemaker cells just fire off automatically, creating that steady rhythm. when a nerve or heart cell needs to fire, those ion channels open and the ions rush across. that sudden shift is the electrical signal. next time you hear a heartbeat, remember its just ions doing their thing.

yeah so, musicians sample older songs basically by taking a slice of an existing recording and turning it into part of a new one. I’m pretty sure the process is more of a collage than a full reproduction. You grab a beat, a horn riff, a vocal lick, a bass line, or a drum break from an old record, then you clean it up, cut it into loops, and layer it over new production. That’s the short version, but there’s a lot going on under the hood.

A lot of it starts with the source itself. Producers dig through crates, digital libraries, or public archives to find something that sparks an idea. Once they have the clip, they’ll isolate it, trim the edges, and maybe change the pitch or tempo so it fits the new track. This is where it gets interesting, because you aren’t copying the song so much as recontextualizing a fragment. A four-bar drum break from a 70s soul record can become the foundation for a hip-hop beat. A vocal ad-lib from a jazz track can be stretched, reversed, or chopped into a rhythmic hook. A melody snippet can be pitch-shifted into a completely different key.

The legal side is messy and worth acknowledging, even in a casual note. Some sampling is cleared, some isn’t, and in some cases a producer gets called out later. I’m not a lawyer, but that tension between borrowing and ownership is part of why the practice remains so hot. Artists argue it’s a fair-use kind of homage, rights holders say they need to be credited and paid. It’s a real debate, and it shapes how people approach the craft.

I like thinking of it as musical remix culture in action. The old recording doesn’t have to be a perfect fit; often the point is to break it down and rebuild it. You can loop a two-second drum hit, reverse a vocal, run it through effects, and suddenly something familiar starts sounding new. That’s the whole trick: take the recognizable fragment, transform it, and make it part of your own composition.

What I find most interesting is how a short piece of an old song can carry a lot of emotional weight. When you hear a familiar snippet in a new context, it connects to the original era or vibe. That recognition is what makes sampling so effective, and why producers spend so much time hunting for just the right clip.

yeah tbh i kept it, i know it's not perfect. the space bar rattles and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. the e key also glitches sometimes and i end up with eexample instead of example, so i have to backspace. it happens maybe once an afternoon, always when i'm typing fast and not looking. i paid $38 and kept it anyway because of the switches. i asked the seller what they were and the answer took a week. by then i had already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. my old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison. my job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. that mattered more than the rattle. sending it back would mean paying for postage and boxing it up, and i'd still be without a keyboard while waiting. so it stays on the desk, and i tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.
